subject: Application of SCR to arboreal lizard data

messages.author: 82efca874eed7d60
messages.subject: Application of SCR to arboreal lizard data
parts:
Hi all,

I am new to SECR and want to confirm its applicability to my data and sampling method.

I want to calculate sex-specific spatial patterns (mainly density, home range, dispersion) for an arboreal, gliding lizard (Draco dussumieri). 

Here’s the sampling details-

I sampled three areca nut plantations (unequal size) with 17 surveys in each plantation.

I surveyed each plantation 1-2 times a week, scanning each tree and noting down GPS coordinates of the tree on which an individual was spotted, along with the sex and ID of that individual.

Each survey was time constrained and I randomized the path taken.

I also took GPS coordinates of all the trees in all three plantations.


Potential caveats-

Some of the edge individuals also utilize forest which I couldn’t sample due to multiple challenges.

In two of the plantations I couldn’t achieve 100% marking so for those two the data is a mix of marked and unmarked. (Considering using SMR model for these two)


I am a bit unsure whether I can use SCR for analysis so posting in this group.

Additionally, in case it can be used, can the trees act as traps (average spacing of trees is 2 to 3 m) or should I adopt the polygon search method?

I also measured perch height of the individuals while sampling so was wondering if the detection probability can be modeled using perch height as a covariate?


I would be really grateful if it could be addressed and also if any further clarifications are required.


Thank you!

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: Application of SCR to arboreal lizard data
parts:
Hello
This is an interesting study and there's a lot to think about, but you seem to be on the right track. 

Edge individuals are accommodated by spatial capture-recapture if you know (can map) the extent of potential habitat outside the study area.

Were lizards marked before you started the surveys? You imply (almost) all individuals were marked. Then it's worth thinking what you want out of spatial capture recapture. Fitting a density surface model allowing for movements?

Whether to use trees as notional 'detectors' is largely a matter of taste and practicality. I would say 'yes' if possible. Often it's easier to discretize polygons rather than use the polygon detector type, but the original Royle & Young 2008 horned lizard dataset is a counter example. GPS error may become an issue.

My feeling is that perch height is useful only if you document the available perch heights (perhaps as a covariate of 'tree'), and maybe not even then. Sex differences in perch height can be analysed outside the capture-recapture analysis.

I hope that others weigh in with their thoughts.

Murray
